words.meaning: Break something into its parts and show how the parts work together.
words.example: Analyse how the writer builds tension in the opening chapter.

words.meaning: Judge how good, useful or successful something is, and give reasons for your judgement.
words.example: Evaluate the effectiveness of the government's response to the crisis.

words.meaning: Give the main features of something in detail. You are not judging it.
words.example: Describe the structure of a plant cell.

words.meaning: Make something clear by giving reasons or showing how it works.
words.example: Explain why the price of housing rose in this period.

words.meaning: Look at more than one side of an idea before reaching a view.
words.example: Discuss whether the law achieves justice for victims.

words.meaning: Show how two or more things are similar, and usually how they differ.
words.example: Compare the two experiments' results.

words.meaning: Show how two or more things are different from each other.
words.example: Contrast life in the city with life in the country.

words.meaning: Give the main points only, without the detail.
words.example: Outline the three stages of the water cycle.

words.meaning: Name or point out exactly what something is. A short answer is enough.
words.example: Identify two features of a persuasive text.

words.meaning: Give the exact meaning of a term — where its limits are.
words.example: Define 'opportunity cost'.

words.meaning: Show clearly how two things are different from each other.
words.example: Distinguish between weather and climate.

words.meaning: Look closely at something and say what you find.
words.example: Examine the causes of the Great Depression.

words.meaning: Decide how important, valuable or successful something is, and say why.
words.example: Assess the impact of social media on teenagers' sleep.

words.meaning: Explain what something means, especially data, a source or a text.
words.example: Interpret the trend shown in the graph.

words.meaning: Give the main ideas briefly, in your own words.
words.example: Summarise the article in three sentences.

words.meaning: Give reasons that show your answer or choice is the right one.
words.example: Justify your choice of method.

words.meaning: Show clearly that something is true, usually by using evidence or an example.
words.example: Demonstrate how the formula is applied.

words.meaning: Make an idea clear by giving an example. (It does not mean 'draw a picture'.)
words.example: Illustrate your point with an example from the text.

words.meaning: Put ideas from several sources together to make one new whole.
words.example: Synthesise the findings of the three studies.

words.meaning: Judge the strengths and weaknesses of something carefully.
words.example: Critique the artist's use of colour.

words.meaning: Support a claim with evidence so it stands up.
words.example: Substantiate your argument with data from the table.

words.meaning: Use what you know to work out what happens beyond the data you have.
words.example: Extrapolate the population trend to 2050.

words.meaning: Suggest an explanation that can be tested.
words.example: Hypothesise why the plants in the dark grew taller.

words.meaning: Put an idea, plan or question into a clear, careful form.
words.example: Formulate a research question for your investigation.

words.meaning: Put forward an idea or plan for others to consider.
words.example: Propose a solution to the traffic problem.

words.meaning: Say what you think should be done, and why.
words.example: Recommend a strategy for the business to increase sales.

words.meaning: Add more detail to an idea you have already given.
words.example: Elaborate on your second reason.

words.meaning: Judge the worth or quality of something.
words.example: Appraise the reliability of this source.

words.meaning: Show what makes two things different. (In Maths Methods it also means 'find the derivative'.)
words.example: Differentiate between mass and weight.

words.meaning: Sort things into groups that share features.

words.meaning: Put things in order of importance, most important first.
words.example: Prioritise the three risks for the committee.

words.meaning: Work out an answer by reasoning from what you already know.
words.example: Deduce the missing angle from the information given.

words.meaning: Work out something that is not stated directly, using clues.

words.meaning: Check that something is sound, accurate or acceptable.

words.meaning: How much, or how far, is something true? Your answer must take a position, not just describe.

words.meaning: The main point a writer argues for — what they want you to accept.
words.example: The writer's contention is that phones should be banned in class.

words.meaning: The central argument of your essay, usually stated in the introduction.
words.example: Your thesis should answer the question directly.

words.meaning: An idea you accept as true and build your argument on.
words.example: The argument rests on the premise that all students have internet at home.

words.meaning: Facts, data or quotations that show your point is true.
words.example: Support each idea with evidence from the text.

words.meaning: An argument against your own — you raise it so you can answer it.
words.example: A strong essay deals with the counterargument.

words.meaning: A result or meaning that follows from something, without being said directly.
words.example: Discuss the implications of the new policy for small business.

words.meaning: As a result of what was just said.
words.example: Rainfall fell sharply; consequently, the crop failed.

words.meaning: Looking at it the opposite way round.
words.example: City rents rose. Conversely, country rents fell.

words.meaning: After that; later.
words.example: The law passed in 1975 and was subsequently amended twice.

words.meaning: Prove that an argument is wrong.
words.example: She refutes the claim with evidence from the census.

words.meaning: Admit that part of the other side's argument is fair, before answering it.
words.example: The writer concedes that the cost is high, but argues it is worth paying.

words.meaning: Making sense as a whole, with ideas that fit together logically.
words.example: A coherent essay answers one question from start to finish.

words.meaning: Held together by words and phrases that link sentence to sentence.
words.example: Linking words such as 'however' make writing cohesive.

words.meaning: Your answer to an argument against you.
words.example: The final paragraph is a rebuttal of the opposing view.

words.meaning: A block of sentences developing one idea.
words.example: Start a new paragraph for each new point.

words.meaning: Put two things side by side so the difference between them stands out.
words.example: The film juxtaposes the wedding with the funeral.

words.meaning: The general direction data moves in over time.
words.example: The graph shows an upward trend in temperature.

words.meaning: A relationship where two things change together. It does not prove one causes the other.
words.example: There is a strong correlation between study hours and results.

words.meaning: A part compared with the whole, often written as a fraction or percentage.
words.example: A large proportion of the sample was under 20.

words.meaning: Big enough to matter. In statistics it means the result is unlikely to be chance.
words.example: The difference between the groups was significant.

words.meaning: Go up and down repeatedly, without a steady direction.
words.example: Prices fluctuated throughout the year.

words.meaning: A period where a value stops changing and stays level.
words.example: Growth rose quickly, then reached a plateau in 2019.

words.meaning: A fall or decrease over time.
words.example: There was a steady decline in newspaper sales.

words.meaning: Happening slowly, in small steps.
words.example: The graph shows a gradual increase, not a sudden jump.

words.meaning: How big something is — its size or scale.
words.example: An earthquake of magnitude 6.5 struck the region.

words.meaning: Something that can change, and that you measure or control in an experiment.
words.example: Temperature was the independent variable.

words.meaning: The middle value when all values are put in order.
words.example: The median house price was $780,000.

words.meaning: How values are spread out across a range.
words.example: The distribution of scores was close to normal.

words.meaning: Growth that gets faster and faster as the amount gets bigger.
words.example: The population showed exponential growth after 1950.

translations.vi: đường, có khả năng hoạt động

words.meaning: How far a value moves away from the average.
words.example: The standard deviation tells you how spread out the data is.

words.meaning: Build up in amount over time.
words.example: Sediment accumulates at the mouth of the river.

words.meaning: A value or result that does not fit the pattern.
words.example: The reading of 92 is an anomaly and should be checked.

units.name: Hedging — showing how certain you are

words.meaning: Something that usually happens, but not always.
words.example: There is a tendency for prices to rise before Christmas.

words.meaning: Show or point to something — weaker than 'prove'.
words.example: The results indicate a link between sleep and memory.

words.meaning: Point towards a conclusion without proving it. Very common in academic writing.
words.example: The evidence suggests that the trend will continue.

words.meaning: Probably true or probably going to happen.
words.example: Rain is likely in the afternoon.

parts.meaning: in a way that can be

words.meaning: A reasonable case can be made for this, though others may disagree.
words.example: This is arguably the poet's finest work.

words.meaning: Mainly; more than any other reason.
words.example: The decline was primarily caused by drought.

words.meaning: Possibly, in the future — it could happen but has not yet.
words.example: The change is potentially damaging to small businesses.

words.meaning: Easy to see; or seeming true but perhaps not really true.
words.example: It became apparent that the sample was too small.

parts.meaning: in a way that can be

words.meaning: Probably, judging by what we know — though it has not been checked.
words.example: The author, presumably writing in 1890, describes the city.

words.meaning: Large and important enough to matter.
words.example: There was a substantial increase in demand.

words.meaning: So small that it can be ignored.
words.example: The effect on the result was negligible.

words.meaning: Neither large nor small; in the middle.
words.example: The study found a moderate improvement in scores.

words.meaning: Mostly; the largest part.
words.example: The population is predominantly under 30.

parts.meaning: in a way that can be

words.meaning: It is possible to imagine this, though it is not likely.
words.example: The result could conceivably be explained by measurement error.

words.meaning: Name the source where an idea or quotation came from.
words.example: Cite the author and year for every quotation.

words.meaning: You can trust it — it gives the same result again and again.
words.example: A single blog post is not a reliable source.

words.meaning: Sound and well founded — it really measures or shows what it claims to.
words.example: The conclusion is valid only if the sample was random.

words.meaning: Not leaning towards one side.
words.example: Try to find an unbiased account of the event.

words.meaning: The point of view a person writes or speaks from.
words.example: The diary gives a soldier's perspective on the battle.

words.meaning: Evidence made at the time by someone who was there.
words.example: A letter written in 1915 is a primary source.

words.meaning: An account written later by someone who was not there.
words.example: Your textbook is a secondary source.

words.meaning: How far a source deserves to be believed.
words.example: The author's expertise adds to the credibility of the report.

words.meaning: Support a claim with a second, independent source that says the same.
words.example: Two other witnesses corroborate her account.

words.meaning: Using someone else's words or ideas as if they were your own. It is cheating.
words.example: Referencing your sources protects you from plagiarism.

words.meaning: Put someone else's idea into your own words. You still name the source.
words.example: Paraphrase the passage rather than quoting all of it.

words.meaning: Saying who an idea, quotation or image came from.
words.example: The image was used without attribution.

words.meaning: Check that something is true.
words.example: Verify the figure against the official statistics.

words.meaning: Based on facts, not on personal feelings.
words.example: A report should be objective.

words.meaning: Based on personal feelings or opinions.
words.example: 'Beautiful' is a subjective judgement.

words.meaning: One of the things that causes or affects a result.
words.example: Cost was the main factor in the decision.

words.meaning: One part or side of something you are looking at.
words.example: Consider the economic aspect of the problem.

words.meaning: A general idea.
words.example: The concept of supply and demand is central to economics.

words.meaning: A standard you judge something against. Plural: criteria.
words.example: Cost was one criterion; safety was another.

words.meaning: A structure of ideas used to organise thinking about a topic.
words.example: Use the four-step framework to analyse the case.

words.meaning: A basic rule or truth that other ideas are built on.
words.example: The principle of equality before the law.

words.meaning: Something that happens and can be observed. Plural: phenomena.
words.example: El Niño is a weather phenomenon.

words.meaning: A testable prediction you make before an experiment. Plural: hypotheses.
words.example: State your hypothesis before collecting data.

words.meaning: The whole approach and set of methods used in a study, and why they were chosen.
words.example: The methodology section explains how the data was gathered.

words.meaning: How important something is, and why it matters.
words.example: Explain the significance of the 1967 referendum.

words.meaning: A conclusion you reach from clues rather than from a direct statement.
words.example: Make an inference about the writer's attitude.

words.meaning: The situation around something, which helps explain it.
words.example: Read the quotation in the context of the whole speech.

words.meaning: A limit on what you can do.
words.example: Time was the biggest constraint on the project.

words.meaning: A fixed limit or setting within which something works.
words.example: The task set clear parameters for the design.

words.meaning: The reasons behind a decision or design.
words.example: Explain the rationale for your choice of materials.

words.meaning: General agreement among a group.
words.example: There is scientific consensus that the climate is warming.

words.meaning: Make up or form something.
words.example: Women constitute 51 per cent of the population.

words.meaning: Be made up of; consist of.
words.example: The parliament comprises two houses.

words.meaning: Get or come from a source.
words.example: The word derives from Latin.

words.meaning: Weaken something gradually.
words.example: The scandal undermined public trust in the company.

words.meaning: Make something easier to happen.
words.example: Good roads facilitate trade between regions.

words.meaning: Make something bad less severe.
words.example: Planting trees can mitigate the effects of heat.

words.meaning: Make a bad situation worse.
words.example: The drought exacerbated food shortages.

words.meaning: Make room for something, or change to fit someone's needs.
words.example: The design accommodates wheelchair users.

words.meaning: Give out a share of something, such as money or time.
words.example: The government allocated $2 million to the program.

words.meaning: Say what caused something, or who made it.
words.example: The scientists attribute the rise to human activity.

words.meaning: Follow a rule, standard or expected pattern.
words.example: The building must conform to safety standards.

words.meaning: Match or be equal to something else.
words.example: Each number corresponds to a name on the list.

words.meaning: Be a sign for; mean.
words.example: In this graph, the dotted line denotes the average.

words.meaning: Include a wide range of things.
words.example: The course encompasses both theory and practice.

words.meaning: Support something from below; be the base of an idea.
words.example: These values underpin the whole legal system.

units.name: Units 1 & 2 — Data analysis, probability and statistics

words.meaning: Data that names a group rather than measuring an amount, such as eye colour.
words.example: Suburb is a categorical variable.

words.meaning: Data that is a number you can count or measure.
words.example: Height in centimetres is numerical data.

words.meaning: How many times a value appears in a set of data.
words.example: The frequency of the score 7 was four.

words.meaning: A column graph for numerical data, where the columns touch.
words.example: Draw a histogram of the class's test scores.

words.meaning: The same shape on both sides of the centre.
words.example: The distribution of heights was roughly symmetric.

words.meaning: Not symmetric — the data has a longer tail on one side.
words.example: Income data is usually positively skewed.

words.meaning: A value that sits far away from the rest of the data.
words.example: The value 210 is an outlier in this data set.

words.meaning: One of the three values that cut ordered data into four equal groups.
words.example: The upper quartile was 78 marks.

words.meaning: The value below which a given percentage of the data falls.
words.example: A score in the 90th percentile beats 90% of students.

words.meaning: A measure of how spread out the data is around the mean.
words.example: A small variance means the scores are close together.

words.meaning: A relationship between two variables.
words.example: Is there an association between hours of sleep and marks?

words.meaning: How likely something is, from 0 (never) to 1 (certain).
words.example: The probability of rolling a six is one sixth.

words.meaning: Modelling a real situation, often by repeating a random experiment many times.
words.example: Use a simulation to estimate the probability.

words.meaning: Making a straight line when graphed; changing by the same amount each step.
words.example: Distance against time gave a linear graph.

words.meaning: The number in front of a variable, which multiplies it.
words.example: In 5x, the coefficient is 5.

words.meaning: Put a number in place of a letter in a formula.
words.example: Substitute x = 3 into the equation.

words.meaning: A group of numbers and letters with no equals sign.
words.example: 3x + 7 is an expression, not an equation.

words.meaning: A statement that two things are equal, using an equals sign.
words.example: Solve the equation 2x + 1 = 9.

words.meaning: A statement that one thing is bigger or smaller than another.
words.example: The inequality x > 5 means x is greater than 5.

words.meaning: Two or more equations that must both be true at the same time.
words.example: Solve the simultaneous equations to find where the lines cross.

words.meaning: A comparison of two amounts, written like 3 : 2.
words.example: Mix the concrete in the ratio 1 : 3.

words.meaning: The small raised number showing how many times to multiply.
words.example: In 2⁵, the exponent is 5.

words.meaning: The power you must raise a base to in order to get a number.
words.example: The logarithm of 100 to base 10 is 2.

words.meaning: A rule that builds each new term from the one before it.
words.example: Recursion lets you find each year's balance from last year's.

words.meaning: A list of numbers in order, made by a rule.
words.example: 3, 6, 12, 24 is a geometric sequence.

words.meaning: How steep a line is — how much it rises for each step across.
words.example: A gradient of 2 means the line rises 2 for every 1 across.

words.meaning: Where a graph cuts an axis.
words.example: The y-intercept is where the line crosses the y-axis.

words.meaning: The U-shaped curve you get from a squared relationship.
words.example: The path of a thrown ball is a parabola.

words.meaning: A line a graph gets closer and closer to but never touches.
words.example: The curve has an asymptote at x = 0.

words.meaning: A pair of numbers giving a point's position, such as (3, 5).
words.example: Plot the coordinate (2, −4).

words.meaning: One of the four regions the axes cut a graph into.
words.example: The point (−2, 3) lies in the second quadrant.

words.meaning: The curve you get when two quantities multiply to a constant.
words.example: As speed rises, time falls along a hyperbola.

words.meaning: Going straight up and down.
words.example: The y-axis is the vertical axis.

words.meaning: Going flat across, left to right.
words.example: Draw a horizontal line through y = 4.

words.meaning: A change that moves, turns, flips or resizes a graph or shape.
words.example: This transformation shifts the graph two units up.

words.meaning: Stretching or squashing a graph or shape.
words.example: A dilation by factor 2 makes the shape twice as wide.

words.meaning: Sliding a graph or shape without turning it.
words.example: A translation of 3 units right.

words.meaning: A set of steps you follow in order to solve a problem.
words.example: Follow the algorithm to find the shortest route.

words.meaning: One repeat of a step that is done over and over.
words.example: After three iterations the value settles.

words.meaning: A selection where the order does not matter.
words.example: How many combinations of 3 students from 10?

words.meaning: Multiplying a number by every whole number below it, written 5!.
words.example: 5 factorial is 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120.

words.meaning: A rule that gives the next term from the one before.
words.example: Write a recurrence relation for the balance each month.

words.meaning: A route that returns to where it started.
words.example: The tour forms a cycle through all six towns.

words.meaning: In a network, the number of edges meeting at a point.
words.example: Vertex B has degree 3.

words.meaning: Where each connection carries a number, such as a distance or cost.
words.example: In a weighted graph the numbers show travel time.

words.meaning: Where connections only go one way, shown by arrows.
words.example: A one-way street system is a directed graph.

words.meaning: Where connections work both ways.
words.example: A friendship network is usually undirected.

words.meaning: The distance all the way around the outside of a shape.
words.example: Find the perimeter of the rectangle.

words.meaning: The distance around the outside of a circle.
words.example: The circumference is π times the diameter.

words.meaning: How much space a solid takes up.
words.example: Calculate the volume of the cylinder.

words.meaning: The total area of all the outside faces of a solid.
words.example: Find the surface area of the box.

words.meaning: Same shape, different size — all lengths in the same ratio.
words.example: Similarity means the angles stay equal.

words.meaning: Exactly the same shape and size.
words.example: The two triangles are congruent.

words.meaning: The longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle.
words.example: Use Pythagoras to find the hypotenuse.

words.meaning: The maths of the sides and angles of triangles.
words.example: Use trigonometry to find the height of the tower.

words.meaning: A direction given as an angle clockwise from north.
words.example: The ship sailed on a bearing of 135°.

words.meaning: When one half of a shape matches the other half.
words.example: A square has four lines of symmetry.

words.meaning: A measurement of size in one direction, such as length or width.
words.example: Give the dimensions of the room.

words.meaning: The number you multiply by to enlarge or reduce a shape.
words.example: A scale factor of 3 makes every length three times longer.

words.meaning: Data about one variable only.
words.example: A histogram displays univariate data.

words.meaning: Data about two variables, so you can look for a relationship.
words.example: A scatterplot displays bivariate data.

words.meaning: The variable you think does the explaining — it goes on the x-axis.
words.example: Hours of study is the explanatory variable.

words.meaning: The variable you think is affected — it goes on the y-axis.
words.example: Test mark is the response variable.

words.meaning: What is left over: the gap between an actual value and the predicted one.
words.example: A residual plot shows whether a straight line fits.

words.meaning: Using logs to straighten out data that curves.
words.example: A logarithmic transformation made the plot linear.

words.meaning: A pattern that repeats at the same times each year.
words.example: Ice-cream sales show a strong seasonal pattern.

words.meaning: Remove the seasonal pattern so the real trend shows.
words.example: Deseasonalise the quarterly figures before finding the trend.

words.meaning: Averaging nearby values to make a bumpy graph clearer.
words.example: Use three-point moving mean smoothing.

words.meaning: Predicting beyond the range of the data you actually have. It is risky.
words.example: Predicting 2050 from 10 years of data is extrapolation.

words.meaning: Predicting inside the range of the data you have. Safer than extrapolation.
words.example: Estimating the value at year 5 is interpolation.

words.meaning: One thing actually making another happen. An association alone never proves it.
words.example: Correlation does not prove causation.

units.name: Unit 3 AOS 2 — Recursion and financial modelling

words.meaning: The loss in value of something as it gets older or is used.
words.example: The van loses $3,000 a year in depreciation.

words.meaning: A rise in the value of something over time.
words.example: The house showed steady appreciation.

words.meaning: An investment or loan paid off by equal regular payments.
words.example: She bought an annuity paying $500 a month.

words.meaning: An annuity that pays out forever, because only the interest is taken.
words.example: The scholarship is funded in perpetuity.

words.meaning: Interest paid on the interest already earned, as well as on the original amount.
words.example: Compound interest makes savings grow faster each year.

words.meaning: The original amount borrowed or invested, before any interest.
words.example: The principal on the loan was $20,000.

words.meaning: How much is left in an account or owing on a loan at a given time.
words.example: The balance after two years was $12,400.

words.meaning: One of a series of equal regular payments.
words.example: He repaid the loan in 36 monthly instalments.

words.meaning: The real yearly rate once compounding is counted, so you can compare loans fairly.
words.example: The effective annual rate was 6.17%.

words.meaning: Paying a debt down to zero through regular payments — literally 'killing it off'.
words.example: The amortisation table shows the balance after each payment.

words.meaning: Where interest is charged only on what is still owing, so it falls over time.
words.example: A reducing balance loan costs less than a flat rate.

words.meaning: Growing or shrinking by multiplying by the same number each step.
words.example: Compound interest produces geometric growth.

words.meaning: A rectangular table of numbers set out in rows and columns. Plural: matrices.
words.example: Write the costs as a 3 × 2 matrix.

words.meaning: One single number inside a matrix.
words.example: The element in row 2, column 3 is 7.

words.meaning: A line of numbers going down a matrix.
words.example: The second column shows the prices.

words.meaning: Swap the rows and columns of a matrix over.
words.example: The transpose of a 2 × 3 matrix is 3 × 2.

words.meaning: The matrix that undoes another one, like dividing undoes multiplying.
words.example: Multiply by the inverse to solve the equations.

words.meaning: A single ordinary number, used to multiply every element of a matrix.
words.example: Multiply the matrix by the scalar 4.

words.meaning: A matrix that has no inverse.
words.example: A singular matrix cannot be used to solve the system.

words.meaning: A number worked out from a square matrix that tells you if an inverse exists.
words.example: If the determinant is zero, there is no inverse.

words.meaning: A matrix showing how things move between states from one step to the next.
words.example: The transition matrix shows customers switching brands.

words.meaning: The steady state a system settles into and then stops changing.
words.example: After many steps the population reaches equilibrium.

words.meaning: A matrix used to rank players or teams by who beat whom.
words.example: Use a dominance matrix to rank the five teams.

words.meaning: An arrangement where the order does matter.
words.example: A permutation matrix reorders the rows.

units.name: Unit 4 AOS 2 — Networks and decision mathematics

words.meaning: A diagram of points joined by lines, showing how things connect.
words.example: Draw a network of the roads between the six towns.

words.meaning: A point in a network. Plural: vertices.
words.example: This network has five vertices.

words.meaning: Next to each other — joined directly by one edge.
words.example: Vertices A and B are adjacent.

words.meaning: A route that starts and finishes at the same vertex.
words.example: Find a circuit that uses every edge once.

words.meaning: Where you can get from any point to any other point.
words.example: The network is connected, so every town is reachable.

words.meaning: A network you can draw flat with no edges crossing.
words.example: Redraw the graph to show it is planar.

words.meaning: A network you can trace in one go without lifting your pen or repeating an edge.
words.example: The network is traversable because only two vertices are odd.

words.meaning: A set of edges that reaches every vertex with no cycles.
words.example: The minimum spanning tree gives the cheapest cabling.

words.meaning: A network with two groups, where edges only run between the groups.
words.example: Matching workers to jobs is a bipartite problem.

words.meaning: Assigning each worker or resource to one task at least total cost.
words.example: Use the Hungarian algorithm to find the best allocation.

words.meaning: Which tasks must be finished before another one can start.
words.example: The precedence table shows task C follows A and B.

words.meaning: On the longest path through a project — any delay here delays everything.
words.example: Task D is on the critical path.

subjects.name: Kinematics
subjects.subtitle: Physics · motion, graphs & trigonometry — build each word!

words.meaning: How fast something moves AND the direction it moves in.
words.example: The car's velocity was 20 m/s heading north.

words.meaning: How fast something moves, without saying the direction.
words.example: Her running speed was 5 metres per second.

words.meaning: The total length of the path something travels.
words.example: The distance around the oval is 400 metres.

words.meaning: The straight-line distance and direction from the start point to the end point.
words.example: My displacement from the door is 2 metres.

words.meaning: How long something takes, measured in seconds, minutes or hours.
words.example: The trip took a time of 3 hours.

words.meaning: How quickly velocity increases (speeding up).
words.example: The rocket's acceleration pushed us back into our seats.

words.meaning: How quickly velocity decreases (slowing down).
words.example: Braking caused a sharp deceleration.

words.meaning: Where something is located compared to a fixed point.
words.example: Her position is 5 metres from the wall.

words.meaning: The line or course along which something moves (e.g. north, left).
words.example: The wind changed direction suddenly.

words.meaning: The state of moving; a change of position over time.
words.example: The ball was in constant motion.

words.meaning: How steep a line is; the slope of a graph.
words.example: A steep gradient means the object is speeding up quickly.

words.meaning: The point where a line crosses an axis of a graph.
words.example: The y-intercept shows the starting position.

words.meaning: Making or relating to a straight line.
words.example: The graph was linear, so the speed stayed constant.

words.meaning: The steepness of a line; another word for gradient.
words.example: The slope of the line tells you the velocity.

words.meaning: Staying the same; not changing.
words.example: Uniform motion means the speed never changes.

words.meaning: Not moving; being still.
words.example: The ball was at rest before I kicked it.

words.meaning: A push or a pull that can change how something moves.
words.example: A force was needed to stop the trolley.

words.meaning: All the input values (x-values) a function can take.
words.example: The domain of the graph is time from 0 to 10 seconds.

words.meaning: A rule that links each input to exactly one output.
words.example: Distance is a function of time.

words.meaning: A function built from different pieces over different intervals.
words.example: The piecewise graph was flat, then sloped upward.

words.meaning: A quantity that can change or take different values.
words.example: Time is the variable on the horizontal axis.

words.meaning: How strongly two variables are related.
words.example: There is a positive correlation between time and distance.

words.meaning: Greater than zero; going up or to the right.
words.example: A positive gradient means the object moves forward.

words.meaning: Less than zero; going down or to the left.
